about: Source of truth for the tutor's knowledge base. `python -m director.knowledge build` (or first use) turns it into SQLite. Facts are paraphrased; `source` is a chapter/tutorial-level pointer. A fact with a `check` is re-computed by the named calculator at build time and only then marked verified; every other fact is 'sourced' (cited, not machine-checked). Misconception `claim` regexes flag wrong statements in model explanations (sentences with a negation are skipped). The 'Spot the Scam' concepts (smishing ... protective actions) cite U.S. consumer-protection guidance (FTC, CISA, FCC); their demo is a FICTIONAL message and its warning signs come from a heuristic prototype (scam.detect), not a trained classifier.

concepts.name: Voltage
concepts.summary: The electrical push between two points, measured in volts (V).

concepts.name: Current
concepts.summary: How much electric charge flows past a point each second, measured in amperes (A).

concepts.name: Resistance
concepts.summary: How strongly something opposes current, measured in ohms (Ω); a resistor is a part made to have a set resistance.

concepts.name: Ohm's law
concepts.summary: Current through a resistor equals the voltage across it divided by its resistance: I = V / R.

concepts.name: Electrical power
concepts.summary: The rate a part converts electrical energy (to heat, light, ...): P = V × I, in watts (W).

concepts.name: Series circuits
concepts.summary: Parts connected end to end in one loop: one current flows through all of them and their voltages add up.

concepts.name: Parallel circuits
concepts.summary: Parts connected across the same two points: each gets the same voltage and their currents add up.

concepts.name: LED
concepts.summary: A light-emitting diode: it conducts in one direction and glows brighter with more current.

concepts.name: Forward voltage
concepts.summary: The nearly constant voltage across a conducting LED (or diode).

concepts.name: Current limiting
concepts.summary: Setting a safe current, usually with a series resistor, so a part like an LED is not destroyed.

concepts.name: Transistor
concepts.summary: A part where a small control signal switches or controls a larger current.

concepts.name: BJT (bipolar junction transistor)
concepts.summary: A current-controlled transistor: a small base current lets a larger collector current flow.

concepts.name: MOSFET
concepts.summary: A voltage-controlled transistor: the voltage on its insulated gate switches the drain current.

concepts.name: Voltage divider
concepts.summary: Two series resistors that split a voltage: V_out = V × R2 / (R1 + R2).

concepts.name: Social engineering
concepts.summary: Manipulating people (with trust, fear or urgency) into giving away information or access.

concepts.name: Suspicious links
concepts.summary: Links in unexpected messages that may lead to look-alike pages or malware.

concepts.name: Impersonation
concepts.summary: A scammer posing as a trusted organization, such as your carrier or bank.

concepts.name: Credential theft
concepts.summary: Stealing login details (password, PIN, one-time code) to take over an account.

concepts.name: Smishing (scam texts)
concepts.summary: Phishing by text message: a fake text that pushes you to tap a link, reply or share details.

concepts.name: Account verification
concepts.summary: Checking an alert yourself through an official channel you open, never through the message.

concepts.name: Protective actions
concepts.summary: What to do with a scam text, and the recovery steps if you already shared something.

facts.text: Voltage is the difference in electrical potential between two points: the push that drives charge around a circuit, measured in volts (V).
An ideal battery keeps a fixed voltage across its terminals; the rest of the circuit decides how much current flows.
Current is the rate at which electric charge flows past a point, measured in amperes (A); a milliamp (mA) is a thousandth of an amp.
Current is not used up: in one loop, the same current that leaves the battery comes back to it. Parts convert energy, not current.
Conventional current is drawn flowing from + to −, opposite to the way the electrons actually move.
Resistance measures how strongly a part opposes current, in ohms (Ω). A resistor is made to have one set resistance.
A resistor's color bands encode its value: two digits, a multiplier, and a tolerance band.
Ohm's law: the current through a resistor equals the voltage across it divided by its resistance, I = V / R.
At the same voltage, more resistance means less current, and less resistance means more current.
A 9 V source across a 1,000 Ω resistor drives 9.0 mA.
Electrical power is the rate energy is converted: P = V × I, in watts (W). A resistor turns its power into heat.
A resistor's power rating must be higher than the power it dissipates, or it overheats; small through-hole resistors are commonly rated 1/4 W.
A 9 V source across a 1,000 Ω resistor dissipates 81 mW in the resistor.
In a series circuit the parts form one loop, so the same current flows through every part.
In a series loop the voltages across the parts add up to the source voltage.
Resistances in series add: the total is R1 + R2 + ...
In a parallel circuit every branch connects across the same two points, so each branch gets the same voltage.
The branch currents in a parallel circuit add up to the total current drawn from the source.
The combined resistance of resistors in parallel is always less than the smallest one, because each branch adds another path for current.
Parallel branches work independently: opening one branch does not switch the others off, which is why household outlets are wired in parallel.
An LED conducts in one direction only, from the anode (+, the longer leg) to the cathode (−, the shorter leg by the flat edge).
An LED's brightness follows its current: more current gives more light, up to its rating.
A typical 5 mm indicator LED is rated for about 20 mA of continuous current.
Once an LED conducts, the voltage across it stays close to its forward voltage, which depends on its color (red LEDs need less than blue or white ones).
This tutor's model treats the LED as a fixed 2 V drop; a real LED's voltage rises slightly as its current increases.
Because an LED's voltage barely changes once it conducts, nothing in the LED itself limits the current; a series resistor has to set it.
The series resistor takes the rest of the supply voltage and sets the current: I = (V_source − V_LED) / R.
With a 9 V battery, a 2 V red LED and a 330 Ω resistor, the current is about 21.2 mA.
With the same battery and LED, a 1,000 Ω resistor lowers the current to 7.0 mA, so the LED is dimmer.
Without a current-limiting resistor an LED draws far more current than it is rated for and is quickly damaged.
A transistor can work as an electronic switch: a small control signal turns a much larger load current on or off.
To switch a load from a logic pin, the transistor usually goes between the load and ground (a low-side switch).
A BJT is current-controlled: in its active region the collector current is about β times the base current, with β often around 100.
A silicon BJT's base-emitter junction drops about 0.7 V while it conducts.
To switch a BJT fully on, designers give it more base current than the minimum, often about a tenth of the collector current.
Switching an LED with a 330 Ω load from a 9 V supply and a 5 V logic pin, the BJT gets a 1,800 Ω base resistor and about 2.4 mA of base current.
A MOSFET is voltage-controlled: its gate is insulated, so it draws essentially no steady current; current flows only briefly while the gate charges.
A logic-level MOSFET turns fully on from a logic pin's voltage and then acts like a very small resistance between drain and source.
BJTs are cheap and work from small voltages but need steady base current; MOSFETs need almost no drive current and usually waste less power as switches.
Two resistors in series split the source voltage; the output across R2 is V_out = V_source × R2 / (R1 + R2) when nothing draws current from it.
With a 9 V source and two 10 kΩ resistors the output is 4.50 V, half the source voltage.
Anything connected to a divider's output draws current and pulls the output voltage below the formula's value.
A voltage divider should not be used to power a device: the load current also flows through R1, wasting power as heat, and the output sags.
Smishing is phishing by text message: a text that pretends to come from a company you trust so that you tap a link, reply, or share account or payment details.
Common scam-text lures are fake fraud or sign-in alerts, package delivery problems, unpaid tolls, and prize or refund offers.
Warning signs of phishing include urgent or emotional language, requests for personal or financial information, and misspelled or look-alike addresses.
This lesson's warning signs come from a keyword heuristic prototype, not a trained classifier: it gives no calibrated probability and can miss new wording or flag real alerts.
Social engineering manipulates people rather than computers: the attacker uses trust, fear or urgency so the victim hands over information or access.
Pressure to act right away is a warning sign: a short deadline or a threat leaves no time to check whether a message is real.
Scammers impersonate companies you know, such as your carrier, bank or a delivery service, copying their names and the tone of real alerts.
A company name in a text can be faked, so the name alone does not prove who sent the message.
Credential theft means tricking someone into giving away login details such as a password, PIN or one-time code, so the thief can sign in as them.
With someone's carrier account details, a thief can try to move their phone number to a SIM the thief controls (SIM swap or port-out fraud) and then receive their text-message codes.
A link in an unexpected text can open a fake page that collects whatever you type, or install malware.
Look-alike addresses mix a familiar name with words like verify, secure or login; the safe habit is to skip the link and open the official app or a website you type yourself.
To check an alert, contact the company using a phone number or website you know is real, such as its official app or the number on your bill, not the contact details in the message.
Forwarding a scam text to 7726 (SPAM) reports it to your wireless provider so it can block similar messages; then delete it.
Don't reply to an unexpected text or tap its links; report it and delete it instead.
If you gave a password away, change it right away, along with any account that reused it, and turn on multi-factor authentication.
If a scammer may control your phone number, contact your carrier from its official number and change your account password; ask about protections against SIM swaps and port-outs.
Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov; if ID numbers such as a Social Security number were taken, IdentityTheft.gov gives a recovery plan.

misconceptions.wrong: The LED or resistor uses up current, so less current returns to the battery.
misconceptions.correction: In one loop the current is the same everywhere; the parts convert energy (to light and heat), not current.

misconceptions.wrong: The resistor has to go before the LED (on the + side) to protect it.
misconceptions.correction: In a series loop the same current flows everywhere, so the resistor limits it equally on either side of the LED.

misconceptions.wrong: A battery always supplies a fixed current.
misconceptions.correction: A battery supplies a (roughly) fixed voltage; the circuit's resistance decides how much current flows.

misconceptions.wrong: A bigger resistor lets more current through.
misconceptions.correction: At the same voltage, more resistance means less current (I = V / R).

misconceptions.wrong: If the battery voltage equals the LED's forward voltage, no resistor is needed.
misconceptions.correction: An LED's current changes steeply with tiny voltage changes and batteries vary, so the current still needs something to set it, such as a resistor.

misconceptions.wrong: A MOSFET needs a steady gate current to stay on, like a BJT's base current.
misconceptions.correction: A MOSFET's gate is insulated: it needs voltage, and current flows only while the gate charges.

misconceptions.wrong: Adding a resistor in parallel increases the total resistance.
misconceptions.correction: A parallel branch gives current another path, so the total resistance goes down and the total current goes up.

misconceptions.wrong: A voltage divider is a good way to power a device from a lower voltage.
misconceptions.correction: A load on a divider's output draws current and pulls the voltage down, and R1 wastes power as heat; use a regulator to power things.

misconceptions.wrong: A link that starts with https or shows a padlock is safe.
misconceptions.correction: https only means the connection is encrypted; scam sites use it too. Skip the link and open the official app yourself.

misconceptions.wrong: If a text uses your carrier's name or your name, it must be real.
misconceptions.correction: Names are easy to copy. Check the alert through the official app or the number on your bill.

misconceptions.wrong: Scam texts are easy to spot because they are full of typos.
misconceptions.correction: Many scam texts are well written and copy real alerts; judge a text by what it asks you to do, not its spelling.

misconceptions.wrong: Replying STOP to a scam text is a safe way to make it stop.
misconceptions.correction: Any reply tells the scammer your number is active; report the text to 7726 (SPAM) and delete it instead.

misconceptions.wrong: Your carrier may text you a link that asks for your password or PIN to verify your account.
misconceptions.correction: Treat any text link that asks for a password or PIN as a scam; check your account in the official app or call the number on your bill.
